short: A tall stone pillar tapering to a pyramid.
note: A tall, four-sided stone pillar that tapers toward a small pyramidal top.
A long, low couch, often without a back or arms.
short: A low couch or cushioned seat.
A curved sword with one cutting edge.
note: A sword whose blade curves and has its cutting edge on the outer, convex side. The name is traditionally applied to several kinds of Middle Eastern and Asian swords.
Stone cut into squared blocks with finished faces for building walls.
short: Squared stone cut for regular masonry.

note: An old term for a light musket or flintlock firearm.
short: An old term for a light musket.

note: A reddish or orange variety of zircon used as a gemstone.
short: A reddish or orange zircon gemstone.

note: Describing a triangular sail hung from a long, slanting yard.
short: A triangular sail on a slanting yard.

note: Persistently demanding attention or making requests in an intrusive way.
short: Persistently or annoyingly demanding.
A tip, gift, or alms.
note: Money given as a gratuity, gift, or alms; from Persian bakhshīsh, a gift.

short: Possibly Arabic Allāhu aʿlam: God knows best.
note: Possibly a rendering of Arabic Allāhu aʿlam, “God knows best,” a formula acknowledging the limits of human knowledge.

short: An Ottoman title for a governor or other high official.
note: A title of rank held by high civil or military officials in the Ottoman Empire, including provincial governors; from Turkish paşa.

short: The Ottoman court or central government.
note: The Sublime Porte: the court or government of the Ottoman Empire. The expression comes through French from the Turkish name meaning High Gate.

short: The Ottoman sultan’s elite infantry.
note: An elite corps of the Ottoman sultan, originally recruited largely from Christian boys taken as tribute, converted to Islam, and trained for military service.

short: The Garden of Bliss, an Islamic name for paradise.
note: Arabic for the Garden of Bliss or Delight. The related plural expression jannāt al-naʿīm, Gardens of Bliss, appears in the Qur’an for the paradise promised to the faithful.

short: A figure in the Arabian Nights.
note: Yunus the Scribe and the Caliph Walid bin Sahl is a tale in The Thousand and One Nights, included in volume seven of Richard Burton’s translation.

sources.label: The Thousand and One Nights · Burton, volume 7

short: A hero of the Arabian Nights.
note: Gharib and his brother Ajib are the title figures of a long adventure in The Thousand and One Nights. Richard Burton’s translation places its conclusion in volume seven.

sources.label: The Thousand and One Nights · Burton, volume 7

short: A legendary city in the Arabian Nights.
note: The City of Brass is a tale in The Thousand and One Nights about an expedition that encounters an extraordinary abandoned city and the remains of vanished power.

sources.label: The Thousand and One Nights · The City of Brass

short: The Egyptian god associated with death and the afterlife.
note: An Egyptian funerary god and ruler of the underworld, commonly shown in a close-fitting mummiform garment and a tall atef crown.

short: The crocodile god of ancient Egypt.
note: An Egyptian god represented as a crocodile or a man with a crocodile’s head, associated with water and fertility and sometimes joined with the sun god as Sobek-Re.

short: A form of the name Seth, the Egyptian god.
note: Sutekh, also called Set or Seth, an ancient Egyptian god associated with desert lands and disorder.

short: The great hero of the Persian Book of Kings.
note: Rustam, or Rostam, a central hero of Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh (Book of Kings), renowned for extraordinary strength and his adventures with his horse Rakhsh.

short: A traditional Persian image of beloved and lover.
note: Rose and nightingale form a longstanding pair in Persian poetry and decorative art: the beautiful rose represents the beloved, and the nightingale the yearning lover or poet.

short: A Muslim religious teacher or learned leader.
note: A Muslim religious teacher or leader, also used as a respectful form of address for such a person. The word comes through Persian from Arabic mawlā, master.

short: A legendary realm of spirits in Persian-inspired literature.
note: A fabulous land of spirits, fairies, and demons in Persian-inspired literature. Isaac D’Israeli’s Romances places the peris and divs there.

sources.label: Isaac D’Israeli · Romances, University of Michigan edition
